title: Design a Versioned Model Rollout Control Plane
prompt:
Design the control plane for deploying versioned inference models to several regions. A model artifact moves through validation, canary, gradual rollout, rollback, and retirement. Online serving systems must continue using the last approved version if the control plane is unavailable.

Specify model/artifact identity, evaluation gates, region and hardware compatibility, rollout ownership, configuration propagation, rollback, and audit trails. Cover how you distinguish a bad model, a bad serving build, and a regional capacity failure. Include capacity admission, SLOs, safety/quality monitoring, and the correctness boundary between the control plane and request-serving data plane.

Do not design model training or assume all regions can host every model.

response.placeholder: Start with an immutable release manifest and the safe behavior when the control plane is down.
response.reference_answer:
## Release identity and approval

A release manifest names immutable model weights, tokenizer, runtime image, evaluator/policy revisions, supported accelerator classes, configuration schema, and signatures. Promotion creates a new manifest rather than mutating a serving tag. Offline validation records both quality and safety gates against a pinned evaluation suite; approval is an auditable transition with required reviewers and explicit override reasons.

## Control plane versus data plane

The control plane owns desired state and rollout policy. It publishes signed, versioned assignments to regional deployment controllers. Serving replicas cache their last verified assignment and continue serving it during a control-plane outage; they never fetch arbitrary model bytes on a request path. A regional controller reports observed version, readiness, capacity, and health using an ownership epoch so an old controller cannot reintroduce a retired release.

## Rollout and rollback

First qualify a release on compatible hardware, then route a bounded cohort by deterministic request key. Advance only when traffic, latency, error, safety, and quality guardrails remain within predeclared bounds. Keep the prior known-good assignment resident while a canary runs. Rollback changes desired traffic and replica assignments through a higher-epoch transition; a replica acknowledges only after loading, warming, and passing local checks. Rollbacks are fast routing/configuration changes, not artifact deletion.

## Failure diagnosis and capacity

Tag every request with release, runtime build, region, hardware class, and routing generation. Compare canary versus baseline on matched traffic where possible. A quality/safety regression correlated with weights indicates a model release issue; errors confined to one runtime build indicate serving software; saturation or queue growth in one region indicates capacity or placement. Admission control uses the currently observed safe capacity, per-tenant limits, and compatible-fleet availability rather than a global average.

## Operations and retirement

Monitor readiness, load time, assignment convergence, route share, inference latency, error codes, safety classifier results, quality proxy drift, capacity headroom, and rollback time. Retire an artifact only after no active or rollback assignment references it and its retention window expires. Keep manifests and approvals for audit, with access controls that separate release operators from model artifact writers.

## Progressive Hints

1. A release is more than a weight file.
2. Serving must fail safely when the controller cannot be reached.
3. Keep the rollback target deployable until promotion is truly complete.
4. Include routing generation in every diagnostic record.
